concepts.decision: Select layered controls from asset value, threat, safety, privacy, and operational need; assign monitoring and response ownership.
concepts.definition: The coordinated protection of people, facilities, equipment, media, and environmental conditions through physical layers and operations.
concepts.failureExample: Installing devices with no monitoring or maintenance produces an appearance of protection, not a working control.
concepts.label: Physical Security

concepts.decision: Use where the organization needs early detection or managed approach before access to the facility interior.
concepts.definition: Control at or approaching the property/building boundary that channels, deters, detects, or restricts entry and movement.
concepts.failureExample: A perimeter with unmonitored gaps moves confrontation and detection closer to protected assets.
concepts.label: Perimeter Control

concepts.decision: Layer controls so approach detection, delay, identification, and response suit the site threat and safety conditions.
concepts.definition: The set of outer-boundary measures such as barriers, lighting, gates, exterior entry controls, cameras, and intrusion sensors.
concepts.failureExample: Relying only on a fence without detection or response leaves a breach unnoticed.
concepts.label: Perimeter Security Controls

concepts.decision: Match identity assurance and escort requirements to the area’s risk while preserving safe emergency egress.
concepts.definition: The authorization and controlled flow of people or materials through a defined entrance, using methods such as badges, guards, locks, or visitor procedures.
concepts.failureExample: A locked door with informal tailgating defeats the authorization decision it is meant to enforce.
concepts.label: Entry Control

concepts.decision: Use internal layers to enforce need-to-access after someone legitimately enters the building.
concepts.definition: Controls inside the facility that restrict and monitor movement among rooms, zones, racks, media areas, and sensitive operations.
concepts.failureExample: Treating lobby access as permission for a server room enables lateral physical movement.
concepts.label: Internal Security Controls

concepts.decision: Create zones where access requirements change; document transitions and exceptions.
concepts.definition: A physically bounded area with a defined asset sensitivity, authorized population, entry conditions, and monitoring/response rules.
concepts.failureExample: An undefined “secure area” leaves staff unable to enforce who may enter or escort visitors.
concepts.label: Security Zone

concepts.decision: Place and secure cameras for needed coverage, privacy limits, recording availability, and response use; protect IP-connected cameras as systems.
concepts.definition: Closed-circuit video surveillance used to observe, deter, investigate, or verify activity in a defined field of view.
concepts.failureExample: A camera pointed away from the entry or with unavailable recording cannot corroborate a tailgating event.
concepts.label: Cctv

concepts.decision: Choose sensing appropriate to the environment and connect it to monitored triage and escalation.
concepts.definition: Sensors and alarms that identify unauthorized boundary or zone entry attempts, such as door, motion, beam, vibration, or gate sensors.
concepts.failureExample: A motion sensor with no alarm response only records a problem after the intruder has acted.
concepts.label: Intrusion Detection

concepts.decision: Select controls from environmental hazards and life-safety requirements, with facilities and emergency coordination.
concepts.definition: Physical safeguards that maintain conditions or limit hazards affecting people and equipment, including fire, HVAC, water, and power protections.
concepts.failureExample: An equipment room can remain access-controlled yet fail from heat, smoke, or water.
concepts.label: Environmental Control

concepts.decision: Set monitored thresholds, response ownership, and health checks for each critical sensor.
concepts.definition: Measurement and alerting for conditions such as heat, water, smoke, humidity, or power state so operators can act before damage escalates.
concepts.failureExample: A disconnected water sensor cannot warn responders before a leak damages equipment.
concepts.label: Environmental Monitoring

concepts.decision: Size and test protection against the required outage/transition and identify dependencies such as fuel, maintenance, and transfer equipment.
concepts.definition: Measures such as UPS, generator, conditioned power, and failover that reduce loss or damage from power interruption or quality problems.
concepts.failureExample: A generator with untested transfer switching can still interrupt a critical load during an outage.
concepts.label: Power Protection

concepts.decision: Monitor normal and exception activity, protect logs, and investigate access or device failures through accountable operations.
concepts.definition: Collection and review of access events, alarms, video, visitor records, and device health to detect anomalies and support response.
concepts.failureExample: Disabling alerts for a noisy door without a compensating control leaves a persistent blind spot.
concepts.label: Physical Access Monitoring

misconceptions.claim: A locked door is sufficient for a critical facility.
misconceptions.correction: Critical facilities need layered access, monitoring, environmental, power, fire, maintenance, and response controls.

misconceptions.claim: Physical security logs are unrelated to cyber investigations.
misconceptions.correction: Entry, visitor, device, camera, and environmental evidence can establish presence, timing, and attack paths.

outcome: Given a facility and threat scenario, select layered physical controls, define operational ownership and response, and verify that access, environmental, power, fire, and monitoring measures work together.

sections.body: Physical security can combine site selection, perimeter barriers, lighting, locks, guards, badges, visitor control, mantraps, cameras, intrusion detection, restricted zones, equipment protection, and environmental safeguards. Perimeter security controls manage approach, boundaries, vehicles, people, and initial detection; internal security controls divide and monitor zones, rooms, racks, media, and movement. Layering should reflect threat, asset value, safety, privacy, and operational need; a control that creates unsafe egress or an unmonitored exception can introduce new risk. Define who monitors, responds, maintains, and reviews each layer.
keyPoints: Deterrent, preventive, detective, and response functions should be explicit at both perimeter and internal boundaries.
Critical areas need stronger boundaries and independent monitoring than general work areas.
Safety and emergency egress must not be sacrificed for security convenience.
sections.title: Protect perimeter and internal areas in layers

sections.body: Physical operations include badge lifecycle, visitor and escort procedures, key management, CCTV and alarm health, guard escalation, fire detection and suppression, HVAC, water, power, generator or UPS support, and maintenance access. Test access and environmental controls, protect their logs and management interfaces, and account for single points of failure. Coordinate facilities, security, IT, safety, emergency services, and business owners in the response plan. A failed sensor or reader is a control exception requiring an owner, compensating measure, expiry, and validation.
keyPoints: Physical access events can support logical investigations and must be attributable.
Environmental controls protect availability and safety as well as confidentiality.
Maintenance and emergency access need authorization, supervision, and closure evidence.
sections.title: Operate environmental and physical-access controls

summary: Physical security protects people, facilities, equipment, media, and operations through layered deterrence, prevention, detection, response, and recovery controls that are maintained in their real environment.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.

Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.
